events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 with no information is always tough. All I can say is I'm looking for anything that feels off in today's discussion and I'll be paying close attention to how everyone responds to the first pressure points. If anyone has any read or observation they'd like to share, now's the time to speak up before we get to voting. Let's see how this unfolds.

Noah makes a good point — day one is mostly about tone rather than hard reads. Since there's nothing concrete yet, I think the best we can do is watch for the usual patterns: players who stay aggressively neutral no matter what, or anyone who seems eager to steer the vote toward a low-information target before we've even built a case. I don't have anything solid on anyone at this point, so I'm not going to throw out a random accusation just to seem engaged. I'd rather see how people respond once actual pressure gets applied. If someone comes into today already suspicious of a specific person without explaining where it comes from, that's the kind of thing I'll find interesting. Otherwise, I'm happy to let the first day play out naturally and vote on what we actually see.

I’m Elena. I agree with Noah and Priya that Day 1 is mostly tone and pressure, not hard evidence. I don’t want to manufacture a read just to look active. What I’ll be watching for is whether anyone tries to turn vague “neutrality” into a quick vote without a real reason, or whether someone avoids committing to anything at all. Right now I have no accusation worth making and no solid suspicion. I’d rather hear more from everyone before forming one.

We’ve all been cautious so far, which makes sense with no evidence, but it also gives us little to compare. Priya, you mentioned watching for aggressive neutrality. What would distinguish that from reasonable Day 1 caution in a specific response?

Good question, Amara. To me, the difference comes down to direction and behavior under pressure. Reasonable Day 1 caution looks like someone who engages with points others make, shares their reasoning process, and stays open to changing their mind as information develops. Aggressive neutrality, the kind I'd find concerning, looks like someone who deflects every attempt at substance, avoids committing even to a process, and especially someone who jumps on a bandwagon vote late without having contributed anything beforehand — that's often a player trying to end the day safely on whichever side is winning. It's also worth noting who never gets challenged: if a vague, noncommittal player slides through the whole day because everyone else is absorbing the pressure, that's worth remembering at the vote. Right now, nothing anyone has said reads as hostile to me. Amara asked a focused question, Elena laid out clear standards, and Noah got things moving — all reasonable Day 1 behavior. I don't have a specific suspect at this point, and I'd rather say that honestly than manufacture a weak case just to look engaged. I'll be watching how people behave in the voting reveal most of all, since that's the first real information we get today.

I want to add one dimension nobody has named yet: the players who haven't said a word. We've now heard from Noah, Priya, Elena, and Amara — that's four of us — and Sam, Felix, Omar, and Theo have been completely silent so far. Priya's point about aggressive neutrality is about deflecting, but silence is its own version of that, and it's the cheapest way to avoid scrutiny while letting others carry the day. I'm not saying silence proves anything, because on Day 1 there may be people reading the room before committing. But I don't want silence to be a free pass just because the rest of us are being thorough.

There's also a structural thing worth naming. Four of the five of us who have spoken have spent our time agreeing with each other, which feels productive but actually isn't — agreement generates no information. If all five of us continue to talk about what we're *not* willing to accuse, we're just going to end the day with a random vote because nobody wants to be the one who broke the consensus. I'd rather we spend our remaining turns testing each other on specific behaviors than on general principles.

So here's my own standard, offered openly so you can hold me to it: I have no suspect today and I'm not going to invent one. If nobody gives me a reason to suspect a specific person by voting time, I'll vote for the person whose behavior has been least informative — not because silence equals guilt, but because a vote has to go somewhere and I'd rather it land on an unexamined player than on one of the four of us who have at least shown a reasoning process. That's a tiebreak, not an accusation, and I'll say so plainly.

Theo, you haven't spoken at all yet. What's your read on the room — who do you find least convincing so far, and why? I'd rather hear a genuine answer with no name attached than a non-answer.

I’m here — I was reading before jumping in. Zara, to answer directly: nobody has given me a real scumread yet. If I have to rank who is least convincing, Noah’s opener was the most generic and least committed, but I don’t think that’s meaningful on its own. Priya and Elena at least laid out standards for what they’ll watch, and Amara asked a useful pressure question. Your point about silence is fair, but your proposed tiebreak — voting the least informative player — worries me slightly because it can become a safe way to eliminate a quiet townie without a case. I’d rather vote someone whose behavior actively avoids accountability than someone who simply hasn’t spoken yet. So my current answer is: no accusation, and I’m not voting silence alone. Zara, if you had to choose between voting a silent player and voting someone whose reasoning you disagreed with, which would you pick and why?

Theo, direct answer: I'd pick the silent player — with one condition I want on the record. If you speak and engage substantively before the vote, your silence stops counting against you and I won't target you for it. But if you stay silent through voting, my vote goes to you, because silence gives me zero information to work with, while a reasoned player gives me something I can test tonight. On your challenge that silence is "a safe way to eliminate a quiet townie": I don't buy it any more than voting a weak reasoner is. Both are low-information votes. The difference is that a stated position can be updated by new information; silence cannot.

And on your point about Noah — I don't think generic is the same as suspicious. Noah set the frame and four of us built on it; that's a leader, not a defector. The pattern I'd actually vote on is someone who deflects every attempt at substance and commits to nothing. So far nobody has done that. Several of you committed to explicit standards, which is exactly what I wanted out of today.

One more thing, so nobody is blindsided: my vote tonight will not be random. If nothing concrete emerges, it goes to the least informative player, and I'll say so before the vote rather than after.

Sam, you haven't spoken at all, and Theo and I just disagreed about what silence means — so I want your position on the record before we vote. If you were voting right now, who would you vote for and why? And if you're voting a silent player, name which one and justify it. A name and a reason, not "no comment" — a non-answer here is itself information, and I'd rather you give me the real one.

Zara, direct answer: if I were voting right now, it would be you. This is a weak read, and I'm saying so openly. I'm not voting on silence. Felix and Omar haven't spoken yet, and I won't punish them for that without a reason. My concern with you is specific. You said you'd vote the least informative player, but in your last message you said Theo hasn't spoken at all. Theo posted in e8, disagreed with your tiebreak, and answered your question directly. You also made a conditional threat against Theo's silence when Theo was already speaking. I'd rather vote for a player whose reasoning I can test, and right now that's you.

On your question: I'd pick a player whose reasoning I disagree with over a silent one. Disagreement gives me something to test tonight, and silence gives me nothing. I also don't have a read I trust on Felix or Omar yet. I'm not claiming either is town or mafia. I'll speak about them when they speak.

Sam, I want to correct the record on the specifics, because your case against me rests on two factual claims and both are wrong.

First: my first message (e7) said "Theo, you haven't spoken at all yet." Theo had not spoken. Theo then spoke in e8. My second message (e9) was written after Theo's, and I addressed him as having just disagreed with my tiebreak. The conditional you quote — that Theo's silence stops counting if he engages — came after he had already engaged and been answered. If you read my two messages in order, the threat you're calling contradictory was conditional on something that had already happened. If you read them out of order, that's a reading error, not a behavioral pattern, and I think it's fair for you to hold me to accuracy.

Second: I never proposed that silence should count against Felix or Omar. I named them as silent and said silence isn't proof. Sam, that's the opposite of what you said I did. You built a motive — that I was going to burn a quiet townie — on a position I did not take.

So here is where I actually stand, and I'll put it on the record before the vote, not after:

I am withdrawing my own "least informative player" tiebreak. It was a bad rule, and Felix pointed out the obvious flaw in it: it rewards whoever is quietest and can eliminate a townie for a scheduling reason rather than a case. I don't want my vote to be a scheduling reason. If no one has a case at voting time, my vote goes to me. That is a legitimate vote under the rules, it wastes no townie's life, and it costs the mafia nothing I care about — because if the mafia wants me dead, my vote at me doesn't help them.

That leaves Felix and Omar. Both of you have said nothing. That's not a free pass and I'm not threatening it — it's simply that you are the only players whose behavior has given me zero information, and I've just told you what I'm doing about players who give me zero information. Felix, Omar: if you speak and engage with something either of the others said, you leave the no-information pool permanently, and my vote has no interest in you at all.

Sam, one specific question, and I want a name and a behavior, not a category: if you are voting me, then whose read in this room do you think is *worse* than mine — and if the answer is nobody, say that instead. "No accusation" was a legitimate answer from everyone else today; I'd rather have a clear "I think you're weak because of this specific line" than a case built on a misreading.

Zara, I'll answer directly. If I vote today, it's still you, but I'm holding that more loosely than I did in e10, and I owe you two corrections. In e10 I said you called Theo silent after he had already spoken. Your e7 said that before Theo's e8, so my timeline point was wrong. I also said you proposed counting silence against Felix and Omar. You didn't. You named them as silent and said silence isn't proof. I withdraw both claims.

What I still have is the pattern. In e9 you said a silent player would get your vote if he stayed silent through voting. In e11 you dropped the least-informative tiebreak and said you'd vote yourself if no one has a case. That's a reasonable endpoint, but it came after I pressed you, and the e9 pressure on silent players hasn't been retracted, only moved. Much of e11 also corrects me rather than stating where your vote points if no one builds a case beyond you.

On your question: no one here has a read I'd call clearly worse than yours right now. Noah's opener was generic, but generic isn't a case. So my current answer is weak, and I'd like it tested.

Theo, you challenged Zara's silence standard in e8, and I think that challenge was fair. Do you think her e11 self-vote is a real position, or a way to avoid naming a target?

Sam, direct answer: I think Zara's e11 self-vote is a real position, not merely a way to avoid naming a target. She withdrew a bad tiebreak after you pressed her, admitted the flaw, and put a concrete alternative on record. That is more accountable than doubling down. But I don't think a self-vote is a good town vote: it spends a vote without pressuring anyone, and if everyone did it the mafia would be happy. So I read it as sincere but not helpful. Her earlier pressure on silent players was fair in principle; the problem was the tiebreak, and she corrected it. Your e10 case had factual errors, which you've now withdrawn, and that matters. What remains is a weak behavioral read, and I don't think it is enough to vote her today. I also don't want to reward silence: Felix and Omar still have not spoken. I am not accusing them for silence, but I want their positions on record before the vote. If no case emerges, I would rather vote on the clearest actual behavior than on a corrected misreading. Right now I have no confident scumread. Sam, your willingness to correct the record reduces my concern about you, but it does not create a case on Zara.

Felix here. I've been reading, and I should have spoken earlier instead of letting silence become the topic. I'm not hiding behind it. I don't have a confident read on anyone yet, so I'll say that plainly.

I agree with Theo that Sam's e10 case had factual errors and Sam corrected them, which I credit. I also agree with Theo that Zara's e11 self-vote looks sincere. Still, the part of Zara's play I keep returning to is the e9 standard, where a silent player gets her vote if he stays silent through voting. That was a pressure rule aimed at people who hadn't yet had a chance to be tested, and Sam was right to question it. Zara, I'm not claiming you're mafia. I'm asking whether you think that standard was fair to Theo and Felix at the time, or whether it was a mistake you've now moved past.

For now my vote is not set. I'm looking for a player whose behavior gives me something concrete to weigh, and I'd rather not put a vote on a self-vote or a scheduling reason. If Zara answers that point directly and plainly, I'll update accordingly.

Zara's reversal is reasonable, but e11 contains two claims that concern me: she says Felix pointed out the flaw before he had spoken, and says she never proposed counting silence against Felix or Omar, despite her earlier least-informative-player tiebreak. Those inaccuracies are more concrete than the fact that she changed her mind, though I don't know whether they indicate mafia.

Also, a self-vote doesn't guarantee no townie is eliminated: it could contribute to a majority if others vote the same way. Abstention is allowed if someone genuinely has no preferred target.

Omar, what do you make of Zara's e11 corrections, and who would you currently vote for, if anyone?

Amara, thanks for bringing me in. To answer your question directly: Zara saying in e11 that Felix pointed out the flaw before Felix had even posted is definitely an error, as is the tension around how silence was going to be treated. But looking at the whole picture, that strikes me more as a flustered player getting their notes and names crossed under scrutiny rather than an intentional mafia lie. Town players frequently scramble details when put on the defensive.

That said, I completely agree with your point about the self-vote. Announcing a self-vote is counterproductive for town. It lowers the bar for a consensus elimination, doesn't generate useful pressure, and effectively abdicates town's voting power. If a player genuinely has no solid target at the end of the day, abstaining is far safer than putting a vote on themselves that mafia could opportunistically exploit to secure an elimination.

As for Sam, while e10 started with clear timeline errors, Sam's immediate retraction in e12 without ego or doubling down reads genuinely town-motivated. Between the two of them, I see friction and miscommunication rather than a clean scum tell.

Right now, I don't have a confident scumread and would not vote for Zara or Sam based on what has happened so far. I'd rather avoid rushing into a low-confidence elimination today unless a real contradiction emerges.

Elena, in e4 you noted that you wanted to hear more before forming suspicions. We've now had a full back-and-forth involving Zara, Sam, Theo, Felix, and Amara. What is your assessment of the push on Zara, and does anyone's stance so far look problematic to you?

Omar, direct answer: the push on Zara is not strong enough for me to join. Sam’s e10 case rested on timeline and position errors, and Sam withdrew both in e12. I credit that correction, but a case that has to be rebuilt after factual retractions is weak. Zara’s e11 also has real inaccuracies — especially saying Felix had pointed out the flaw before Felix had spoken — and I agree with Amara that a self-vote is not useful town play. But I read that more as a player scrambling under pressure than as a coordinated mafia line. The problematic stances so far are Sam’s initial overreach and Zara’s muddy details, but both have enough explanation that I would not call either a confident scumread. Felix’s late entry was not ideal, though he engaged once here and did not just hide. Theo’s e13 was measured and did not pile on. Amara’s e15 correctly separated concrete inaccuracies from the fact that changing one’s mind is not itself suspicious. Right now I have no accusation I trust. I will not vote Zara on a corrected misreading, and I will not treat the self-vote as a case by itself. If no better target emerges, I would rather abstain than force a low-confidence elimination.

My position is still a weak lean on Zara, not a settled case. Her e9 rule made silence a voting threat before Theo or Felix had any chance to speak. She has since dropped the tiebreak, and Theo is right that her e11 self-vote looks sincere, but it doesn't help town. I also own my e10 errors. I got Zara's e7 timeline wrong and withdrew that claim in e12. On Felix and Omar: I'm not voting for silence, but both still need to be tested. Felix, you said Zara's answer on the e9 standard would move you, and she has already withdrawn the tiebreak. What more would you need from her to keep her on your list, and is there a player you'd rather test instead?

Sam, direct answer: Zara's e11 retraction of the tiebreak and her self-vote are real movement, but I'm not satisfied yet. Her e9 rule made a silent player's vote conditional on staying silent through voting, before Theo or I had any chance to speak, and she hasn't explained why that was fair. Her e11 claim that I pointed out the flaw before I had posted is also an error I'd like her to own. I don't read those errors as proof of mafia, since players under pressure get details wrong, but they add to the e9 problem. I'd keep her on my list until she addresses the e9 standard directly and gives a concrete reason to vote for someone other than herself. Sam, you asked whether I'd rather test someone else. I'd like to hear more from Omar: he called Zara's errors scrambling, but he hasn't said who he'd vote for if no one builds a case by voting time. Theo, you called Zara's self-vote sincere. If she answers the e9 question clearly, does that change your view of her?

Felix, direct answer: yes, if Zara directly addresses the e9 standard — why it was fair to Theo and Felix before either had spoken — owns the e11 claim that Felix had already posted, and names a concrete non-self vote target with reasoning, my view of her improves and I would not vote her today. Sincerity isn’t the issue; accountability is. A self-vote still wastes town’s vote, and abstention is better if no case exists. If she keeps correcting the record without answering the substance, my concern rises, but not enough alone for a confident scumread. I have no confident scumread now.

Omar, Felix asked earlier and I want it on record: if no one builds a case by voting time, who do you vote for, or do you abstain? Name the target or say abstain plainly. Also, you called Zara’s errors scrambling — do you think her e9 silence standard was acceptable at the time? Specific answer, not a category.

Theo, direct answers to your two questions: First, if no compelling case emerges by voting time, I will abstain. I've stated before that manufacturing a vote or relying on a self-vote is dangerous for town, and an abstention is the cleanest way to prevent mafia from manipulating a low-information miselimination on Day 1. Second, no, Zara's e9 silence standard was not acceptable at the time. Imposing a voting threat on players who hadn't spoken yet early in Day 1 ignores normal game pacing and treats silence as guilt, which is bad reasoning. That said, I still separate bad reasoning from mafia intent; her subsequent fluster and retraction in e11 look more like town scrambling than calculated deception. Noah, you opened the day in e2 but haven't commented on any of the back-and-forth between Zara, Sam, and the room. Given the entire debate around Zara's standards and retractions, where do you stand on her, and would you vote or abstain today?

Omar, thanks for bringing me in. I've been absorbing the back-and-forth and you're right that I owe a position.

On Zara: her e9 silence standard was premature and I said nothing then, which is on me. Pressuring players for silence before they've had a fair chance to speak creates exactly the dynamic the mafia wants — a low-information vote on someone who simply hadn't had their turn yet. She corrected the tiebreak in e11, which I credit, but her e11 inaccuracies — claiming Felix had pointed out the flaw before he'd posted, and misrepresenting her own silence position — are real. I read those as scrambling rather than calculated, same as Omar and Elena.

On Sam: his e10 case had errors he immediately withdrew in e12 without ego. That's a point in his favor. His continued lean on Zara after the retractions is weak but not scummy — he's being honest about it being weak.

Where I actually land today: I don't think Zara or Sam warrants a Day 1 elimination. The case against Zara has been repeatedly corrected and the case against Sam was built on factual mistakes. Voting either would be exactly the kind of low-confidence elimination that helps mafia.

My vote today: I'm leaning abstain unless someone gives me a genuinely concrete reason to vote otherwise. The players who concern me most aren't in the center of this debate — they're at the edges. Players who have contributed nothing or who have been perfectly agreeable the entire day. But I'm not willing to vote on silence or agreeableness alone.

What I'd actually like to see before the vote: one person try to articulate a genuine case — not a corrected misreading, not a preference about self-votes, but a specific behavioral reason they think someone here is mafia. If nobody can do that by voting time, abstain is the right call.

A correction to the discussion: Theo had already spoken when Zara made her e9 conditional statement. Her original question to him came before he spoke; the later conditional was awkward, but it wasn't a threat made before he'd had a chance to respond.

Zara's e11 claim about Felix remains an unexplained error, but she has used all three speaking turns, so we shouldn't demand an answer she can't give today. I don't have a strong enough case to vote for her on that alone.

Priya, you've been watching for unchallenged neutrality and late bandwagoning. Has anything in the subsequent discussion changed your assessment, particularly of the emerging preference to abstain?

Amara, since you asked what's changed my assessment: yes, several things, and none of them point where I expected this morning.

The push on Zara has run its course. Sam's e10 case contained two factual errors he withdrew in e12, which I credit — correcting yourself without ego under pressure is exactly the behavior I said I'd be watching for, and it's a point in his favor. Zara's e9 standard was genuinely bad reasoning, and Omar is right that it treated silence as guilt. But her e11 retraction, flawed as it was, is movement in the right direction. My original concern was a player who deflects every attempt at substance and commits to nothing. Zara did neither — she committed, got challenged, and updated. That's not the pattern I flagged, and I won't pretend it is. I also won't vote on scattered details like the Felix timeline error; pressured players scramble specifics, and that cuts both ways for everyone in this thread.

On the emerging abstain consensus, I want to be honest about my own standard. In e6 I said I'd find a late bandwagon toward a low-information target concerning. An everyone-agrees-to-abstain vote is the mirror image of that: it's consensus generating no information, the same failure mode from the opposite direction. I'm not going to manufacture a scumread just to avoid abstaining — that's worse. But I don't want us to treat abstention as virtuous by default. It should be the fallback if no case emerges, not the plan.

So my position: no vote on Zara, no vote on Sam, and I'm genuinely open between abstaining and voting whoever presents the most concrete reasoning by voting time. What I'd need is an actual case, not a corrected misreading — and if nobody builds one, I'll abstain rather than force a low-confidence elimination.

Felix, you said in e19 you'd keep Zara on your list until she addressed the e9 standard and owned the e11 error — but she's out of turns and can't respond. So I want your position stated plainly before the vote: with Zara unable to answer, do you vote her anyway, move your vote elsewhere, or abstain? And if you'd vote her without that answer, I'd like to hear why an unanswerable standard still earns a vote.

Priya, direct answer: Zara's e9 standard was a mistake, and I said so in e19. But she has no speaking turns left to answer it, and her e11 error about my post is a scrambled detail rather than a case. I'm not voting her on that alone today. I'm also uneasy about the abstain consensus forming around Omar's position. Omar, you've called Zara's errors scrambling and framed abstention as the plan, but you haven't named one behavior from today that you're weighing. Sam, your case on Zara was the most aggressive of the day, and it fell apart on timeline errors. I'd like to know whether you still see her as the main pressure point or whether you're now reaching. My vote isn't set. Omar, what specific behavior makes you comfortable abstaining instead of testing the players who have been tested least?

Felix, to answer your question directly: I am not framing abstention as an ideal goal for town, but as the only disciplined fallback when every substantive push today collapsed under factual review.

The two main pressure points today were Sam's case on Zara and the scrutiny on Zara's silence standard. Looking closely at the behaviors: Sam made factual timeline errors in e10, but in e12 he retracted them completely without defensiveness, ego, or shifting goalposts. That is authentic town accountability, not mafia pushing a manufactured miselimination. Zara's e9 condition was flawed logic, but her scramble in e11—including mistaking when you had posted—reads as genuine fluster under pressure rather than calculated mafia deception.

What makes me comfortable abstaining rather than 'testing the least-tested players' at the ballot box is the structure of Day 1. With nine players, an elimination requires five votes. Throwing votes at someone simply because they haven't been in the crosshairs turns the day into a blind guessing game, offering the mafia a low-information miselimination without requiring them to expose themselves on a real argument. Testing players belongs in discussion; the voting phase is for executing an elimination when there is genuine suspicion.

If someone had exhibited predatory opportunism—such as piling onto Zara once she scrambled or trying to revive Sam's retracted points—I would vote for them. Instead, what we saw was friction resolving through corrections. Forcing a low-confidence elimination under these circumstances gives mafia an unearned advantage. Unless a concrete contradiction emerges from Noah or Elena's final turns, abstaining remains the safest, most disciplined play for town.

I have no confident scumread today. The push on Zara weakened once Sam withdrew the timeline and position claims in e12, and I agree with Theo and Omar that her later scramble reads more like fluster than a clean mafia tell. I also would not vote Sam now: his immediate correction under pressure is a town-leaning behavior, not a case. I will not treat a self-vote or silence alone as grounds for elimination. If no concrete behavioral case emerges before voting, I will abstain rather than force a low-confidence vote.

Noah, you said in e22 that the players who concern you most are at the edges — those who contributed nothing or were perfectly agreeable — but you did not name one. Please name the specific edge player you are weighing and one behavior from today that makes them more concerning than Zara or Sam, or say plainly that you have none. I want that on record before the vote.

Elena, direct answer: I don't have one. My e22 comment about players at the edges was honest concern but vague, and you're right to call it out before the vote. Let me put this plainly on record: I cannot name a specific behavior from Felix or Omar that makes them more concerning than Zara or Sam today. They entered late, but both engaged substantively when asked — Felix directly addressed my question in e14 and Omar answered Theo's in e21 with specific positions. Late entry alone isn't a case, and I won't pretend it is.

So my e22 framing was too broad. What I was actually feeling was that the room has converged so neatly around abstention that nobody has really been tested — but that's a criticism of the day's structure, not a reason to vote any individual. I agree with Priya's e24 point that an everyone-agrees-to-abstain vote is consensus generating no information, and I agree with Omar's e26 point that forcing a low-confidence elimination helps mafia. Both are true, and they pull in opposite directions.

Where I land: I have no behavioral case strong enough to vote for anyone today. If nobody presents a concrete contradiction before voting, I'll abstain rather than manufacture a target. I'd rather have an honest abstain than a vote I can't justify with specific behavior.

One thing I'll note for tomorrow: the players who have spoken the least — Felix, Omar, and to some extent Sam — haven't been examined under real pressure the way Zara has. That's not a vote today, but it's where I'll be looking first on Day 2.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
The vote is tied. Nobody is eliminated.
Night begins.
Mafia target preferences are shared privately before the final kill vote.
Elena is not mafia.
Amara was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Amara's death is a real loss. She kept asking for specific behavior, and her e15 point about Zara's inaccurate claims was a fair test. Mafia may have removed a voice pressing for substance, so we should treat her last questions as still open. Day 1 votes: Zara and Omar each drew two, Felix drew one, and I voted Zara. My vote rested on Zara's e9 silence standard and her e11 errors. I haven't withdrawn it, but I'm honest that my lean is weak, and Zara hasn't answered Felix's and Amara's questions. Omar, my concern with you is specific. In e16 and e21 you called Zara's errors scrambling, and in e26 you defended abstaining as the disciplined fallback. When Felix and Priya asked which behavior you were weighing, your answer described the voting process rather than naming any player's behavior. Elena and Theo both voted for you, and you haven't addressed why. Your abstention framing is the consensus Priya warned about, and it let the room settle without testing the players who hadn't been examined. I'm not calling you mafia, but I want a concrete answer. Noah, you said in e22 that the players at the edges concern you, then named no one in e28. Priya, your e24 point that abstention should be the fallback, not the plan, was right. Day 2 shouldn't end on an unexamined default.

Sam, let's address your points directly. First, you note that Elena and Theo voted for me and say I haven't addressed why. The simple reason is timing: neither Elena nor Theo ever stated in the thread that they intended to vote for me. In e20, Theo asked me two questions, but never indicated he intended to vote me based on my answers. Elena in e27 explicitly said she would abstain if no concrete behavioral case emerged. Their votes were completely untelegraphed prior to the e30 reveal, so there was literally no opportunity to address them before Day 1 ended.

Second, regarding my stance on abstaining: I was completely transparent. In e21 and e26, I stated openly that the cases on Zara and Sam had unraveled under scrutiny, and that forcing an elimination based on retracted arguments was poor play. I stated on the record that I would abstain, and my vote matched my words.

What is truly informative about Day 1's reveal is the disconnect between stated positions and secret ballots across several players:
1. Zara stated in e11 that she would self-vote if no case existed, yet secretly voted Felix.
2. Felix suggested in e25 that he wouldn't vote Zara on the e9/e11 issues alone, yet cast his ballot for Zara.
3. Theo and Elena both spoke about abstention being preferable to low-confidence eliminations, yet quietly placed votes on me without stating a case.

Now, between Elena and Theo, Elena had already noted in e17 that she was skeptical of the push on Zara and was weighing the field. A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
